title: Body weight tendency · FTO
summary: The FTO intron-1 variant rs9939609 is the most robustly replicated common variant for body weight. Each copy of the A allele is associated on average with about 0.4 kg/m2 higher BMI (roughly 1-1.5 kg for an average-height adult) and about 1.3x the odds of obesity. Physical activity and overall diet quality substantially attenuate this association.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, the genotype not associated with the FTO weight effect. On average, TT carriers weigh about 3 kg less than AA carriers. Body weight remains overwhelmingly shaped by energy balance, environment, and hundreds of other variants.
interpretations.AT: One copy of the A allele, associated on average with roughly 0.4 kg/m2 higher BMI and about 1.3x the odds of obesity compared with TT. The effect is modest and is smaller in physically active people in most studies.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of A, found in about 16% of people with European ancestry. This group averages about 3 kg more body weight and about 1.7 times the odds of obesity than TT. This shifts tendency, not destiny. Many AA carriers are lean, and regular activity weakens the link.

title: Body weight tendency · MC4R region
summary: MC4R is a brain receptor that helps control appetite. Variation near it is the second most consistent common genetic link to body weight after FTO. Each rs17782313 C allele is linked to about 0.2 kg/m2 higher BMI and about 1.1 times the odds of obesity. Some studies also report slightly more hunger and snacking.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, the common genotype not associated with the MC4R-region weight effect. This locus contributes only a small slice of the overall genetic influence on body weight.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the C allele, found in roughly a third of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with about 0.2 kg/m2 higher BMI, a small effect equivalent to well under 1 kg for most adults.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele. Associated on average with about 0.4-0.5 kg/m2 higher BMI and modestly higher odds of obesity compared with TT. This is a small average shift in appetite-related weight regulation, one factor among many hundreds.

title: Type 2 diabetes · TCF7L2
summary: TCF7L2 rs7903146 is the strongest common genetic variant for type 2 diabetes known, acting mainly through reduced insulin secretion. Each copy of the T allele is associated on average with roughly 1.4x the odds of type 2 diabetes; two copies with roughly 2x. Lifestyle factors such as weight, diet, and activity still dominate absolute risk.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, the genotype with the lowest average type 2 diabetes odds at this locus. This does not remove risk from other genetic and lifestyle factors, which together matter far more than any single variant.
interpretations.CT: One copy of T, found in about 40% of people with European ancestry. This result is linked to about 1.4 times the odds of type 2 diabetes versus CC, mainly through slightly lower insulin release. Lifestyle changes prevented diabetes across all genotypes in trials.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of T, found in about 8% to 10% of people with European ancestry. This result is linked to about twice the odds of type 2 diabetes versus CC. It is the largest known common-variant effect for this condition. Even so, most TT carriers do not develop diabetes. Weight and lifestyle strongly shape actual risk.

title: Type 2 diabetes · PPARG Pro12Ala
summary: PPARG helps control fat-cell growth and insulin response. Pro12Ala (rs1801282) was one of the first type 2 diabetes variants confirmed across studies. The common C allele makes proline and is linked to slightly higher odds. Each G allele makes alanine and is linked to about 15% lower odds and slightly better insulin response.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the common proline (C) allele, carried by roughly 75-80% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with modestly higher odds of type 2 diabetes (about 1.25x) relative to alanine carriers. Because the genotype is so common, its individual contribution to risk is small.
interpretations.CG: One proline and one alanine allele. The alanine (G) copy is associated on average with about 15% lower odds of type 2 diabetes and slightly better insulin sensitivity. This is a small protective shift, not a safeguard.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the alanine (G) allele, an uncommon genotype (about 1-2% of people of European ancestry). Associated on average with the lowest type 2 diabetes odds at this locus and modestly better insulin sensitivity. Other genetic and lifestyle factors remain far more influential overall.

title: Type 2 diabetes · KCNJ11 E23K
summary: KCNJ11 makes part of a potassium channel that triggers insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. rs5219 changes amino acid 23 from glutamate to lysine. Each lysine copy, the T allele on the GRCh38 forward strand, is linked to about 1.15 times the odds of type 2 diabetes. It slightly lowers insulin release.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele (glutamate, E23), the most common genotype. Not associated with the modest reduction in insulin secretion linked to the K variant at this locus.
interpretations.CT: One copy of the T allele (lysine, K23), carried by roughly 45% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with about 1.15x the odds of type 2 diabetes compared with CC — a small effect, dwarfed by weight, age, and family history.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele (lysine, K23), found in roughly 12% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with about 1.3x the odds of type 2 diabetes compared with CC, via subtly reduced insulin secretion. This is one small factor within a highly polygenic and lifestyle-sensitive condition.

title: Fasting glucose · MTNR1B
summary: MTNR1B encodes a melatonin receptor expressed in pancreatic beta cells, linking circadian signaling to insulin release. Each copy of the G allele at rs10830963 is associated on average with about 1.3 mg/dL (0.07 mmol/L) higher fasting glucose and roughly 1.1x the odds of type 2 diabetes.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, the common genotype, not associated with the MTNR1B fasting-glucose effect. Fasting glucose is shaped by many dozens of loci plus weight, sleep, and diet.
interpretations.CG: One copy of the G allele, carried by roughly 40% of people of European ancestry. Associated on average with about 1.3 mg/dL higher fasting glucose and slightly higher odds of type 2 diabetes — a small shift well within normal day-to-day variation, measurable only across large populations.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele. Associated on average with about 2.5 mg/dL higher fasting glucose and roughly 1.2x the odds of type 2 diabetes compared with CC. A routine blood test tells far more about actual glucose regulation than this genotype does.

title: Insulin resistance · IRS1 region
summary: IRS1 helps pass insulin signals inside muscle and fat cells. The common rs2943641 C allele near IRS1 is linked to less insulin sensitivity and higher fasting insulin. Each copy is also linked to about 1.2 times the odds of type 2 diabetes. Unlike many diabetes variants, it acts through insulin response rather than insulin release.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, found in roughly 14% of people of European ancestry. This genotype is associated on average with better insulin sensitivity and the lowest type 2 diabetes odds at this locus.
interpretations.CT: One copy of each allele. The C allele is associated on average with slightly reduced insulin sensitivity and modestly higher fasting insulin; the effect per copy is small relative to the impact of weight and physical activity on insulin action.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, the most common genotype (roughly 40% of people of European ancestry). Associated on average with reduced insulin sensitivity and about 1.2x the odds of type 2 diabetes per C allele relative to TT. Because it is so common, this genotype describes the population average more than an elevated state.

title: Adiponectin levels · ADIPOQ
summary: Fat tissue releases adiponectin, a hormone that helps the body respond to insulin. Levels tend to be lower with obesity and type 2 diabetes. The A allele of the ADIPOQ promoter variant rs17300539 is one of the strongest common genetic links to blood adiponectin. Each copy is linked to higher average levels.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of G, the common genotype in about 85% of people with European ancestry. This group has average adiponectin levels. Body composition also has a large effect, and a blood test can measure the hormone directly.
interpretations.AG: One copy of A, linked to higher average blood adiponectin. Higher levels often track with better insulin response. This variant has a small and less consistent link to later metabolic outcomes than it has to hormone levels.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele, a rare genotype (about 1% of people of European ancestry). Associated on average with the highest adiponectin levels at this locus. This describes an average hormonal tendency; an actual adiponectin or metabolic panel is far more informative for any individual.

title: Saturated fat and body weight · APOA2
summary: The APOA2 promoter variant -265T>C (rs5082) is a much-cited gene-diet finding. APOA2 is read from the reverse strand, so promoter CC appears as GG on the GRCh38 forward strand. In three US groups, GG was linked to about 1.8 times the odds of obesity only when saturated-fat intake was high, at about 22 g per day or more. At lower intake, the genotypes did not differ.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of A, the promoter TT genotype in the original studies. About 40% of people with European ancestry have this result. The studies found no link between saturated-fat intake and body weight for this genotype.
interpretations.AG: One copy of each allele (TC promoter genotype). Behaved like AA in the interaction studies: no detectable difference in obesity odds by saturated-fat intake. Reported associations at this locus apply mainly to the homozygous GG group.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of G, the promoter CC genotype in the studies. About 10% to 15% of people have this result. It was linked to about 1.8 times the odds of obesity only with high saturated-fat intake. At lower intake, the groups did not differ. Gene-diet findings are hard to repeat, so this is an early signal.

citations.label: Corella et al., Arch Intern Med 2009

title: Diet response and body weight · GIPR
summary: GIPR makes the receptor for GIP, a gut hormone released after eating that helps trigger insulin release. The rs2287019 C allele is linked to slightly higher BMI in large studies. In the two-year POUNDS LOST trial, T carriers on low-fat diets lost more weight and had larger gains in fasting glucose and insulin response.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, the most common genotype (roughly 65% of people of European ancestry). Associated on average with very slightly higher BMI in population studies. In the POUNDS LOST trial this genotype showed smaller average improvements on low-fat diets than T carriers — a single-trial finding that needs replication.
interpretations.CT: One copy of T. In POUNDS LOST, T carriers on low-fat diets lost about 1% more weight at six months and had larger gains in fasting glucose and insulin response. The high-fat groups showed no genotype difference. Diet-response genetics is still early, so this result is suggestive, not final.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, an uncommon genotype (about 4% of people of European ancestry). Associated on average with slightly lower BMI in population studies, and in one diet trial with the largest average metabolic improvements on a low-fat diet. These are averages from a single trial arm and should be read as a weak prior, not a prescription.

citations.label: Qi et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012
